item.title: Reimagining Small Business Futures - AI, Inclusion, and Territorial Innovation
item.content:encoded:
Nicola Cucari, Sapienza University of Rome

Guanglei Zhang, Wuhan University of Technology

Jintao Lu, Shanxi University of Electronic Science and Technology

Hua Fan, Shanghai International Studies University

Eric Liguori, Florida State University

The global innovation landscape is undergoing a profound restructuring. Collaboration among geographically distributed innovation ecosystems is intensifying. At the same time, the rapid advancement and diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping the dynamics of global industrial competition. New innovation hubs are emerging across the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, and several emerging economies. In parallel, digital technologies, platformization, and the decentralization of computing power are reducing traditional geographical and scale barriers. As a result, the conditions for competition and innovation are being fundamentally redefined. In this context, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are no longer structurally disadvantaged. Instead, they can increasingly act as agile and innovation-driven players within global value chains.

AI-enabled technologies offer SMEs unprecedented opportunities. They can enhance productivity, improve decision-making, automate processes, and reconfigure business models toward more scalable and data-driven architectures. At the same time, AI adoption poses significant challenges related to investment capacity, skills gaps, cybersecurity risks, ethical concerns, and unequal access to digital infrastructures. Unlike large corporations, SMEs operate as socio-economic infrastructures deeply intertwined with local production systems, community networks, and place-based development trajectories.

This special issue examines how AI can reshape the future of small and medium-sized enterprises through three interconnected lenses: (1) Technological transformation - how SMEs can scientifically adopt and adapt AI technologies and integrate them into daily operations, medium- and long-term development strategies, and business model innovation to achieve technological transformation and sustainable growth; (2) Inclusive innovation - how AI can build a universally beneficial digital ecosystem for diverse entrepreneurial entities and disadvantaged or marginalized entrepreneurial groups to alleviate structural inequalities and promote more equitable and inclusive innovative development; and (3) Territorial and ecosystem development - how AI-enabled SMEs can enhance territorial economic resilience, improve territorial innovation systems, and support the implementation of local intelligent specialization strategies.

Contributions are particularly encouraged that move beyond technology adoption perspectives to explore how AI reconfigures organizational capabilities, entrepreneurial cognition, stakeholder relationships, and value creation mechanisms in SMEs.

Potential topics

  • AI-driven business model innovation in SMEs
  • Digital transformation pathways under technological turbulence
  • AI and sustainable competitive advantage in resource-constrained firms
  • AI-enabled work redesign and organizational reconfiguration in SMEs
  • Inclusive AI ecosystems for minority, women, migrant, and informal entrepreneurs
  • Algorithmic Bias and transparency in AI-assisted SMEs
  • AI-enabled territorial innovation and smart regional development
  • Public policies supporting equitable AI adoption among SMEs
  • AI, cybersecurity, and risk governance in small businesses
  • Human–AI collaboration and entrepreneurial decision-making
  • Data strategies and knowledge management in SMEs
  • Data ownership and territorial digital autonomy in AI-driven SME development
  • Ethical, social, and governance implications of AI adoption
  • AI platforms and SME participation in digital value chains
  • AI for local resilience, crisis response, and adaptive entrepreneurship

  • October 26, 2026: Colloquium Dates

item.title: Bridging digitalisation, sustainability, and resilience through systems thinking tools: Integrated perspectives and collaborative practices for SMEs
item.content:encoded:
Rui Torres de Oliveira, Deakin University

Agnes Toth-Peter, University of Queensland

Martie-Louise Verreynne, University of Queensland

David Audretsch, Indiana University

Domenico Dentoni, MBS School of Business

Andrea Chiarini, University of Verona

The 21st century presents a range of complex and interdependent challenges, including climate change, resource depletion, economic inequality, and technological disruptions. These so-called wicked problems demand a paradigm shift in our approach to problem-solving. Addressing such challenges requires multi-stakeholder partnerships and holistic, systems-level approaches that transcend traditional, siloed methodologies. Systems thinking, a powerful tool for understanding complexity and interconnections, offers a pathway to sustainable solutions.

Although systems theory became foundational in fields such as environmental sciences during the 20th century, its adoption in strategic management research has been more limited. This reluctance may be tied to the enduring influence of reductionist approaches rooted in early scientific management and innovation models. A systems perspective is critical as it views organizations as complex adaptive systems or 'functioning wholes', which contrasts with problem-solving focusing on isolated components. This special collection aims to bring systems thinking methodologies to the forefront and inspire a deeper engagement with systems-based frameworks and tools, advancing both theoretical and practical understanding of their application in business and management contexts, as well as their transformative potential in addressing complex, interconnected challenges.

By shifting away from traditional reductionist approaches, we seek to highlight how systems thinking can uncover hidden dynamics, identify leverage points, and foster innovative solutions at the intersection of sustainability and digitalization. The new technologies of the Industry 4.0 revolution, including data-driven insights, automation and increased transparency, are changing the way businesses operate. However, it is important to better understand the impact of these disruptive innovations as a result of rapidly progressing digital technologies, as they often convey a dark side of digital change in the social and environmental context. This duality highlights the importance of applying systems thinking to ensure that digital transformation aligns with sustainability goals. Within the sustainability domain, the circular economy introduces a new economic system and logic that also fundamentally disrupts business-as-usual. This requires a shift from individual-level innovation to collective solutions, thus relying on an ecosystem and systemic approaches to achieve a whole-of-lifecycle perspective and integrate supply chains to create closed-loop systems. However, existing tools and frameworks often fail to accommodate the complexity of such an interconnected approach, limiting their effectiveness in addressing the challenges of circularity and disruptive digital solutions.

Recent literature increasingly calls for holistic, systems-level assessments and methodologies to address complex sustainability challenges. While 'system change' and 'systems thinking' often appear in the political, industry and academic discourse, these calls have yet to be fully realized. Nonetheless, the superficial adoption of systems thinking, which neglects the tools and methods to uncover underlying feedback mechanisms and behaviour over time, risks creating a façade of systemic awareness while inadvertently exacerbating issues and rebound effects, ultimately worsening the planetary crisis. This online collection seeks to bridge this gap by highlighting innovative research and practices and by advancing our understanding of interconnected systems and the leverage points within them, we can develop more effective business strategies for achieving resilience and sustainable development.

In this call for papers, we emphasize the importance of 'real' systemic change in the contexts of sustainability, digitalization, and resilience. By aspiring to a real system change, we recognize that defining what constitutes a 'real' systemic shift remains a challenging, often contested but also underdeveloped issue, with scholars often using terms such as 'systemic change', 'system change' or 'transformative change', or using 'systems thinking' without the adequate tools and methodologies applied. There is also a variety among the types of systems across disciplines, definitions used and their scale, which makes this even more difficult to clarify. The literature points to examples, such as large-scale system changes that involve both the breadth of engaging large numbers of people, institutions, and geographies, as well as the depth of transforming the complex power structures and relationships within these systems. Cross-sector partnerships navigating wicked problems are often marked by knowledge uncertainty, value conflicts, and complexity, which require adaptable governance processes to continuously reassess the problem over time. Addressing a complex issue often requires assessing the levers and solutions by examining cross-boundary impacts across different systems and sectors. Expanding the boundary can offer additional insights into intervention points, revealing hidden mechanisms or suggesting that the most effective leverage may lie on someone else's patch. Thus, there is a need for new studies and frameworks that capture the complex interactions between actors, partnerships, and societal issues, across different levels, metrics and scales. Together, these perspectives illustrate that 'real' systemic change is not a static, singular transformation, but an evolving process shaped by diverse and often conflicting stakeholder interests, involving cross-boundary and cross-sector connections.

We invite contributions that explore and contribute to the better understanding of 'real' systemic change, through investigating the synergy between systems thinking, sustainability, and digitalisation. Accordingly, this online collection aims to address the urgent need for a paradigm shift in how we conceptualise and tackle grand challenges, building upon cross-sector partnerships and value co-creation, leveraging frameworks like the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), circular economy principles, and the transformative potential of Industry 4.0 and 5.0 technologies. We invite contributors to discover and use a wide range of tools within systems thinking, including but not limited to causal loop diagrams, system archetypes, system maps, system dynamics models, group model building, and participatory methods.

Potential topics

  • Applications of systems thinking tools, such as causal loop diagrams (CLDs), system archetypes, and system dynamics modeling, in addressing sustainability challenges
  • Development and validation of systems-level frameworks and methodologies for sustainable development
  • Case studies demonstrating the impact of systems thinking on real-world sustainability and/or digitalisation initiatives
  • Use of group model building and participatory system dynamics to support interdisciplinary and ecosystem solutions
  • Exploration of system archetypes and system dynamics models to identify leverage points for driving transformational change and to investigate levers in cross-boundary settings
  • The role of digital technologies, including IoT, AI, big data, and blockchain, in enabling systems-level insights and solutions in the circular economy and sustainability initiatives
  • Integration of digitalisation with circular economy strategies and Industry 5.0 principles and potentials
  • Innovative approaches to digital transformation that promote sustainable development
  • Cross-sectoral and interdisciplinary research to foster collaboration in bridging sustainability and digitalisation, using systems thinking
  • The role of ecosystems in sustainable business models and the boundaries of entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Methodologies for recognising, assessing and addressing the interconnectedness of environmental, economic, and social systems
  • Open innovation in new sustainable businesses, considering distinct institutional contexts and economic systems, such as emerging and developed economies

Timeline

  • October 1, 2026: Rolling submissions begin
  • May 31, 2027: Manuscript deadline for rolling submissions

item.title: Novel Forms and Models of Organization
item.content:encoded:
Masatoshi Kato, Kwansei Gakuin University

David Audretsch, Indiana University

Roy Thurik, Erasmus University Rotterdam

Maksim Belitski, University of Reading

Alex Coad, Waseda Business School

Eric Liguori, Florida State University

Rapid technological change, globalization of supply chains and demand, increasing physical and digital connectivity, and inter-dependencies between actors in innovation and entrepreneurial ecosystems are forcing entrepreneurs and managers to rethink how they organize beyond the manufacturing of products and services, how they innovate, what technologies they adopt, and what markets they enter. The forms and models of organization affect a firm's ability to become exceptional. At the core of firm organization, the factors that distinguish them from their counterparts in the industry and region are firm size, firm age, stage of entrepreneurial continuum, institutional context, and technology-savviness. Firms that have been able to optimize their organization will outperform their regional competitors, markets, and industry; create new forms of growth at a different pace; and approach the innovation and production frontier. Through organizations in different forms, entrepreneurs and mature firms create product and process innovation and coordinate people, external ecosystem actors, government, suppliers, and capital to achieve frontier outcomes.

This collection is especially interested in organizational forms enabling rapid growth without compromising productivity, efficiency, and societal impact, and facilitating innovation and market entry, firm resilience, and survival within both firm shocks and exogenous shocks. Moreover, the collection is interested in understanding how firms' high growth, scaling, and exceptional performance are driven by novel organizational forms. This focus is timely for the Journal of Small Business Management as an intellectual platform that studies why and how the most novel forms and models of organization in performance, growth, efficiency, and innovation are emerging in large tech firms and in exceptional performers among micro-, small-, and micro-firms, in social entrepreneurial firms, and even non-profit organizations. The special focus includes the novel forms of organization that allow for persistent steady growth, high value added, and other exceptional performers—such as niche innovators, scaleups, accelerators, blitzscalers, hidden champions, and Mittelstand-type firms and hyperspecialized firms—that repeatedly outperform their counterparts in the industry.

By combining specific forms of organization, these firms often operate nearby or at the innovation and production frontier despite constrained resources and through global or localized resource orchestration. Hidden champions or niche innovators—for example, hyperspecialized digital and non-digital firms that focus on a small set of activities and scale through digital technologies or localized networks and interdependencies with complements and partners often plugging into collaborators' value chains—are highly successful small firms that hold top global market positions in niche segments.

Global outreach is an important locus to understand novel forms of organization. Global firms, such as micro-multinationals or born-global firms, are young and small firms that internationalize early, working with a lean core and extensive external partners for production, distribution, or customer acquisition, and often relying on global value-chain orchestrators. While prior work has examined financial performance, resource management, scaling, and innovation in such firms, most evidence comes from European contexts, with little evidence from other regions of the world. For example, niche leaders in parts of Asia may begin with an imitation strategy and then move up the value ladder. These firms may be more likely to pursue listing and brand recognition, may expand into adjacent domains beyond niche focus, and may balance domestic and global knowledge via investment in training, R&D, and engagement with ecosystem actors regionally and globally. Little is known about how organizational forms differ across regions, industries, countries, and clusters, or which specific characteristics enable them to experiment, adopt, and develop certain forms of organization that ensure their exceptional performance.

This online collection invites work that theorizes and empirically examines novel forms and models of organization, including structures, processes, architectures, institutions, and governance, that enable firms of different ages, sizes, and niche focus to approach or redefine the productivity and innovation frontier. The collection welcomes research that opens the black box of novel forms and models of organization, enabling firms to outperform their close and distant competitors, recombine a variety of knowledge, and adopt new modes of working, hiring, and innovating to achieve exceptional performance. Additionally, the collection welcomes research that explains when, how, and why particular organizational forms and models outperform others across regions, industries, clusters, and ecosystems in diverse contexts of high-cost developed economies, high-cost emerging economies, and other developing economies.

This collection is expected to investigate how novel forms of organization can appear beyond the OECD and WEIRD countries representing Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic societies (primarily North America, Western Europe, Australia, and parts of East Asia like Japan/South Korea). Interestingly, most developed Asian economies have actively identified and cultivated niche leaders and innovators through national programs, such as Japan's Global Niche Top Companies Selection 100 and South Korea's World-Class 300 & Global Specialized Enterprise Cultivation. In China, two policy-driven categories—niche champions and specialized, advanced, differentiated, and innovative firms—aim to move small businesses up global value chains, emphasizing market performance, strategic uniqueness through innovation, competitive advantage, internationalization, and sustainable growth. Understanding new forms and models of organization for innovation and firm growth will create a rich empirical setting and extend existing growth and innovation theories.

Potential topics

  • How do firms adopting novel forms of organization differ in leadership, governance, and decision-making, and how do these differences shape innovation and productivity at the frontier?
  • What internal microstructures (e.g., boards, design, cross-functional teams, routines) enable firms to combine and recombine internal capabilities with external knowledge and ecosystem actors to achieve exceptional performance?
  • How do novel organizational forms affect authority, accountability, and coordination across functions, and what are the effects on innovation speed, product and managerial innovation, value creation, talent retention, growth, and scaling?
  • Which combinations of internal investment (make), external acquisition (buy), and alliance orchestration (ally) constitute novel organizational models that sustain frontier performance across firm types (hidden champions, niche leaders, sustained innovators, blitzscalers, scalers, etc.)?
  • How does the diversity (institutional and geographic) of external knowledge and innovation partners translate into firms adopting novel forms of organization, and what internal routines convert diverse inputs into outcomes?
  • Under what conditions do international vs regional knowledge collaboration and spillovers generate non-redundant knowledge that improves innovation and performance, and how do firms with different organizational forms apply, filter, and integrate this knowledge?
  • How does digitalization (AI and robotics, data systems, cloud, prominent role of intangibles, etc.) reshape internal process architectures, and which organizational forms best convert digital investments into productivity and innovation gains?
  • Which governance models (data rights, intellectual property, cybersecurity, partner contracts) enable novel organizational forms to adopt and scale complex technologies while maintaining trust and control in technology and partners?
  • How do digitally savvy firms pivot and reconfigure organizational forms to build resilience to supply, demand, and geopolitical shocks, and what design features predict faster recovery and sustained innovation?
  • How do firms implement novel forms of organization while embedded in industry and entrepreneurial ecosystems, and how does ecosystem position shape organizational models for innovation and scaling?
  • How do niche leaders and other exceptional performers orchestrate global supply chains as an organizational capability, not only a sourcing choice, across regional and international contexts?
  • What partner portfolio mixes (universities, suppliers, customers, competitors, government, research labs, conferences, competitions, trade and industrial associations, scientific communities) are associated with frontier outcomes, and what form of organization do firms need to adopt to efficiently govern such collaborations, knowledge spillovers, and firm strategies?
  • How do relationships with government shape novel organizational models through procurement, standards, subsidies, and cluster governance, and when do these relationships enhance versus constrain innovation and productivity?
  • How do organizational models vary between emerging and traditional industries and across industrial clusters of novel and emerging industries where traditional forms of organization are no longer working?
  • How do deglobalization pressures and techno-nationalism reshape firms' organizational choices?
  • What distinctive business model configurations characterize exceptional performers across countries, regions, industries, and stages of growth, age, and size, and how are these configurations enabled by organizational form?
  • How do European, Asian, American, and African leaders in WEIRD and non-WEIRD countries differ in adopting and experimenting with novel forms of organization?
  • What contextual factors explain these cross-country differences?
  • Do niche leaders exhibit distinctive innovation patterns (radical vs incremental, product vs process, ecosystem vs standalone), and which organizational designs best explain variation in these patterns and their performance effects?

Timeline

  • November 1, 2026: Manuscript submission opens
  • November 15, 2026: Submission deadline for extended abstracts and full papers
  • January 31, 2027: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Reform to Renewal: Succession, Socioemotional Wealth, and the Future of Chinese Family Businesses
item.content:encoded:
James Vardaman, University of Memphis

Feigu Zhou, University of Montevallo

Eric Liguori, Florida State University

Shuai Jin, Jiangsu University

Weiwen Li, Sun Yat-sen University

The Theories of Family Enterprise Conference is pleased to partner with Jiangsu University to host a special TOFE research colloquium focused on the future of Chinese family businesses (TOFE China). Submissions will be considered for fast-track review and publication in a forthcoming Journal of Small Business Management (JSBM) special collection. This collection is affiliated with a colloquium scheduled for January 9th, 2027, at Jiangsu University in Zhenjiang, Jiangsu Province, China. Scholars from around the world are invited to submit to the colloquium, with a special invitation to scholars who inhabit the Chinese context. The colloquium provides an opportunity for authors to receive developmental feedback directly from JSBM editors and a pathway to publication in the special collection, subject to JSBM's standard peer review process.

The economic reforms initiated in 1978 fundamentally altered the trajectory of private enterprise in China. By loosening restrictions on private ownership and enabling market-oriented activity, the reform era created conditions under which family businesses could emerge, survive, and ultimately become one of the defining organizational forms shaping China's economy. Over the decades that followed, many of these firms evolved from founder-led ventures into large and influential enterprises that now occupy central positions within domestic and global markets.

Yet the historical conditions that enabled the rise of Chinese family firms also create a unique contemporary challenge. As we approach the 50-year anniversary of Reform and Opening, many founder generations are approaching or actively navigating succession. As leadership transfers unfold, questions once centered on founding, growth, and legitimacy are increasingly giving way to questions of continuity, identity, legacy, and preservation.

This timing is particularly important as succession in Chinese family firms raises questions extending beyond ownership transfer or governance design. Succession often involves renegotiating what aspects of the enterprise should endure, what should change, and whose values define the future of the firm. These issues bring socioemotional wealth (SEW) to the forefront.

SEW perspectives suggest family firms pursue goals beyond economic performance, including preserving family control, maintaining family identity, sustaining social ties, protecting emotional attachment to the firm, and ensuring transgenerational continuity. As Chinese family businesses enter second- and third-generation transitions, these noneconomic priorities may become increasingly salient and contested. Founders and successors may differ in the importance they attach to legacy preservation, family influence, entrepreneurial renewal, internationalization, professionalization, and social status.

At the same time, Chinese family firms provide a uniquely important context for advancing family business theory and, in particular, SEW scholarship. Unlike family businesses in many Western economies that have evolved across multiple generations within relatively stable institutional environments, most contemporary Chinese family firms emerged only after China's market reforms and are now experiencing large-scale waves of intergenerational succession. As a result, successors are assuming leadership amid shifts in economic institutions, governance expectations, family structures, and societal values. Traditional Confucian principles emphasizing family continuity, filial piety, and hierarchical authority remain influential, yet these norms increasingly coexist with modern market logics, professional management practices, global stakeholder expectations, and changing attitudes toward gender and inheritance.

This special collection in Journal of Small Business Management seeks research that advances socioemotional wealth perspectives in Chinese family businesses. We welcome conceptual, quantitative, qualitative, mixed-method, and historical approaches.

The generation of Chinese family firms born from the reforms of 1978 now faces a defining moment. As founders transition authority and successors redefine what should endure, Chinese family businesses offer an unparalleled context for understanding how families preserve, adapt, and renew both economic and socioemotional legacies. The goal of TOFE China is to capture this moment and use it to advance a richer theory of family enterprise.

Potential topics

  • Founder succession and leadership transfer in post-reform family firms
  • Successor identity formation and legitimacy
  • Preservation versus erosion of SEW during succession
  • Tensions between family control and professionalization
  • Emotional attachment, family identity, and transgenerational intentions
  • SEW and strategic renewal
  • Long-term consequences of Reform and Opening for family enterprise
  • State–family business relationships over time
  • Family and nonfamily employee experiences
  • Shared identity and organizational identification

Timeline

  • October 15, 2026: Extended Abstract Submission Deadline
  • November 15, 2026: Proposal feedback delivered
  • January 9, 2027: TOFE China Colloquium at Jiangsu University
  • May 1, 2027: Full Manuscript Submission Deadline
  • September 1, 2027: Decisions on first round of submissions
  • March 1, 2028: Second round submissions due
  • June 1, 2028: Decisions on second round of submissions
  • December 1, 2028: Special collection published
